description: I am an independent space enthusiast and legal professional passionate about lunar exploration, space science, technology and the future of human spaceflight. Through LUNAR CHRONOS, I combine research, scientific tools and an original approach to lunar mission planning. I welcome collaborators interested in space engineering, astronomy, software development, data science, scientific validation and mission planning.
summary:
LUNAR CHRONOS is an independently developed lunar mission-planning prototype created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. It integrates interactive lunar mapping, SPICE-based solar geometry, detailed Earth visibility calculations and time-dependent environmental analysis within a unified planning interface focused on the lunar South Pole. 

Users can explore lunar reference locations, select observation dates and times, compare scenarios, examine solar elevation and assess geometric Earth visibility windows over a 708-hour period. Built using Python, React, TypeScript, FastAPI, SpiceyPy and JPL DE440 ephemeris data, the prototype combines scientific computation with accessible visualization and mission-planning tools. 

Its distinctive contribution also includes Cosmic Calendar, Universal Standard Time (UST), an original proposed 13-phase temporal framework for organizing lunar mission timelines alongside local environmental conditions.

LUNAR CHRONOS aims to support preliminary mission analysis, exploration and education while transparently identifying the additional terrain, power and communications modelling required for operational use.
details:
LUNAR CHRONOS

An integrated lunar mission-planning prototype

LUNAR CHRONOS

An integrated lunar mission-planning prototype

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026
Challenge: Lunar Landing Site Navigator
Project developed by: N. Sahra

Explore the Moon. Plan with precision.

Project overview

LUNAR CHRONOS is an independently developed lunar mission-planning prototype with an original proposed temporal framework. It brings together interactive lunar mapping, SPICE-based calculations, solar elevation analysis, Earth visibility geometry, time-dependent visibility analysis, mission-planning tools and a proposed 13-phase timekeeping framework.

The prototype focuses particularly on the lunar South Pole, where illumination conditions, Earth visibility and the timing of surface activities are important considerations for preliminary mission planning.

Its distinguishing conceptual contribution lies in integrating existing scientific and technical capabilities within a common planning environment, complemented by the proposed Universal Standard Time (UST) framework, which was developed from the original Cosmic Calendar concept.

LUNAR CHRONOS is a research and planning prototype. It is not a certified landing-site assessment system, an operational lunar navigation service or a scientifically validated mission operations platform.

Application access and source code

LUNAR CHRONOS is deployed as a hosted web application on Render and can be accessed directly through a web browser.

The application is available at: https://lunar-chronos-app.onrender.com

The public GitHub repository is available at:

https://github.com/LunarChronos27/LUNAR-CHRONOS

It contains the application source code, project documentation and demonstration materials.

Contents

  1. Project concept and response to the challenge
  2. Integrated lunar mission-planning environment
  3. Scientific and technical architecture
  4. Cosmic Calendar — Universal Standard Time (UST)
  5. Preliminary independent computational cross-check
  6. Relevance, original contribution and potential impact
  7. Current limitations and scientific integrity
  8. Future development and progressive roadmap
  9. Use of super-intelligence tools and AI-assisted development
  10. Conclusion — from a lunar prototype to a broader planetary vision
  11. Looking ahead

1. Project concept and response to the challenge

1.1 Origin of the project

LUNAR CHRONOS originated from my own concept of bringing lunar mission planning, environmental observation and time organisation together within a single framework.

I developed the underlying idea and its conceptual direction before undertaking its technical implementation for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, specifically in response to the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge.

The project began as an original approach to examining how lunar location, observation time, solar geometry, Earth visibility and mission activities could be considered together. I subsequently decided to translate this concept into a practical application using available scientific resources, programming technologies and development tools.

The technical implementation proved more achievable than I had initially anticipated. What began as a conceptual idea developed into an independently created lunar mission-planning prototype that brings several complementary capabilities together within one interactive environment.

LUNAR CHRONOS therefore represents both an original project concept and its first practical technical implementation.

1.2 Project objective

The principal objective is to support the preliminary examination and comparison of lunar locations, observation times and environmental conditions, particularly around the lunar South Pole.

The application enables users to explore selected lunar locations, examine solar elevation, investigate the geometric visibility of Earth over time and consider these conditions in relation to mission-planning activities.

It also explores how a proposed temporal framework could complement conventional timekeeping when organising lunar mission timelines.

2. Integrated lunar mission-planning environment

LUNAR CHRONOS combines several complementary capabilities within a single application.

2.1 Interactive lunar mapping

The application provides an interactive lunar map focused on the lunar South Pole.

Selected reference locations include the lunar South Pole region, Shackleton Crater and the de Gerlache vicinity.

The mapping environment uses LROC imagery, including Wide Angle Camera (WAC) and Narrow Angle Camera (NAC) layers, through the LROC mapping service.

These locations provide geographical references for preliminary exploration and comparison. They must not be interpreted as certified landing sites or as locations for which terrain hazards and landing safety have been fully assessed.

2.2 Solar elevation analysis

LUNAR CHRONOS calculates the geometric elevation of the Sun relative to the local lunar horizon for a selected location and time.

This information helps users examine illumination geometry and its potential relevance to mission timing and surface activities.

Solar elevation is an important preliminary parameter when considering illumination conditions. However, it does not, by itself, provide a complete assessment of solar energy availability or power-generation capacity.

A comprehensive solar power assessment would also require consideration of terrain obstruction, surface orientation, panel inclination, irradiance, equipment efficiency, temperature and energy storage.

2.3 Earth visibility analysis

The application examines the geometric position of Earth relative to the local lunar horizon.

The analysis includes Earth-centre elevation, Earth's apparent angular radius, upper-limb elevation and lower-limb elevation.

These parameters help determine the geometric position of Earth in relation to a selected lunar observation point.

The results provide preliminary information relevant to the examination of potential Earth visibility. They do not establish the availability of an operational communications link.

Assessing actual communications availability would require additional analysis of terrain obstruction, antenna orientation, link budgets, equipment characteristics and mission-specific communications constraints.

2.4 Time-dependent visibility analysis

LUNAR CHRONOS includes a time-dependent Earth visibility scan covering a 708-hour period, with hourly sampling.

This feature allows users to examine how the geometric visibility of Earth changes over time and to identify periods that may warrant further investigation.

The resulting information can support the preliminary consideration of observation and mission-planning windows.

The current implementation does not constitute a complete communications-window prediction system. In particular, the analysis does not yet incorporate all terrain, antenna, spacecraft and communications-link constraints.

2.5 Location and scenario comparison

The application provides tools for examining selected lunar locations and comparing relevant geometric results under different location and time conditions.

This supports preliminary scenario exploration and helps users consider how local conditions may differ between reference locations.

These comparison capabilities are intended to assist investigation and planning. They do not replace a comprehensive scientific assessment of landing-site suitability.

2.6 Mission planning and CLPS reference tools

LUNAR CHRONOS includes mission-planning elements and a reference module covering selected Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) missions.

This module provides additional mission context alongside the geographical and environmental analysis.

The CLPS module is a selected mission reference resource rather than an official or exhaustive mission registry. Mission information, including projected launch and operational dates, must be checked against authoritative sources before being used for mission-critical purposes.

3. Scientific and technical architecture

3.1 Computational foundation

The computational environment uses Python, FastAPI and SpiceyPy, together with NASA/JPL SPICE resources and the JPL DE440 planetary and lunar ephemeris.

SPICE-based calculations use relevant lunar orientation and reference-frame information to support the computation of solar geometry and Earth visibility relative to selected lunar locations.

The application uses these resources to derive preliminary geometric results for selected locations and observation times.

The use of authoritative scientific datasets and established computational libraries provides a technical foundation for the prototype. It does not, in itself, establish that every application output has been independently validated.

3.2 Software architecture

The current application combines a Python-based computational backend with a web-based interactive frontend.

The principal backend and computational technologies are Python, FastAPI, SpiceyPy and the JPL DE440 ephemeris with associated SPICE resources.

The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite and OpenLayers to provide the interactive interface and visualisation environment.

The frontend communicates with the backend, which performs the relevant calculations and supplies the resulting data to the application.

3.3 Scientific data and reference frames

The project uses scientific resources associated with NASA/JPL and lunar mapping services.

The treatment of lunar orientation and reference frames is particularly important because observations from a lunar surface location must be related to the Moon's orientation at the relevant observation time.

The current implementation uses SPICE-based calculations and lunar orientation information. The exact reference frames, kernels, correction settings and assumptions used in each calculation must be documented when the results are independently evaluated.

The outputs should therefore be understood as preliminary computational results produced under the application's current configuration.

4. Cosmic Calendar — Universal Standard Time (UST)

4.1 Origin and concept

The Cosmic Calendar is an original timekeeping concept developed by N. Sahra.

Its proposed Universal Standard Time (UST) framework explores an alternative way of organising time into a consistent temporal structure that could be used alongside conventional time references.

The concept was incorporated into LUNAR CHRONOS to examine how a proposed temporal framework might contribute to the organisation of lunar mission timelines.

4.2 Proposed 13-phase framework

UST uses a proposed framework divided into 13 equal temporal phases.

Its purpose is to provide a consistent reference for organising activities and comparing temporal intervals within the application.

The framework is based on a custom epoch and a defined cycle duration. Its current implementation provides provisional UTC-based date and time calculations for assigning temporal labels.

The framework can be described as follows:

A proposed 13-phase temporal framework designed to provide a consistent reference for organising lunar mission timelines alongside local lunar environmental conditions.

4.3 Relationship with UTC and lunar mission planning

UST is intended to complement conventional timekeeping rather than replace it.

UTC remains the authoritative reference for the application's date and time inputs and for the interpretation of scientific and operational data.

UST is a proposed conceptual framework, not an officially recognised lunar time standard. The current implementation also does not establish a complete conversion between UTC and a lunar local time system.

Furthermore, the present version does not implement a leap-second model or establish a physical lunar time scale. Its temporal calculations must therefore be interpreted within the limits of the current provisional implementation.

The integration of UST into LUNAR CHRONOS represents the project's original conceptual contribution: exploring how a proposed temporal organisation system could be associated with lunar mission-planning activities and environmental observations.

5. Preliminary independent computational cross-check

5.1 Purpose of the comparison

A preliminary numerical cross-check was conducted to compare selected LUNAR CHRONOS outputs with independently generated results from NASA/JPL Horizons.

The purpose was to examine whether selected geometric calculations produced numerically comparable results under the configurations used for the test.

This exercise represents an initial verification step rather than a comprehensive scientific validation of the application.

5.2 Test configuration

The comparison used the following configuration: 8 November 2026 at 12:00 UTC, the lunar South Pole as the reference location, a latitude of −90°, a longitude of 0° and a lunar reference radius of 1,737.4 km.

LUNAR CHRONOS used the JPL DE440 ephemeris, whereas the Horizons comparison used JPL DE441.

The two systems did not use identical computational configurations. Their reference frames and calculation settings must therefore be considered when interpreting the numerical differences.

5.3 Numerical results

The following values were recorded during the comparison:

Solar elevation

  • LUNAR CHRONOS: +1.533300°
  • JPL Horizons: +1.533280°
  • Absolute difference: 0.000020°

Earth-centre elevation

  • LUNAR CHRONOS: −6.456700°
  • JPL Horizons: −6.456684°
  • Absolute difference: 0.000016°

For the LUNAR CHRONOS Earth visibility calculation, the recorded angular radius of Earth was 0.9239°.

The corresponding calculated limb elevations were −5.5328° for the upper limb and −7.3806° for the lower limb.

Comparable Horizons limb values were not recorded as part of this test. Consequently, the limb calculations cannot be considered independently cross-checked by this comparison.

5.4 Interpretation and limitations

The numerical differences recorded for solar elevation and Earth-centre elevation are small. However, they must not be interpreted as proof of complete scientific accuracy.

The two systems used different ephemerides and calculation configurations.

The LUNAR CHRONOS calculation used DE440 and the lunar reference frame MOON_ME_DE440_ME421, with geometric SPICE calculations using no aberration correction. It also used a spherical lunar reference and did not incorporate atmospheric refraction or terrain obstruction.

The Horizons comparison used DE441 and a MEAN_ME reference frame, with its own apparent-position calculation settings, including light-time, gravitational deflection and stellar aberration corrections, as well as precession and nutation considerations.

These differences mean that the comparison was not a strict like-for-like test.

A more rigorous validation programme would require harmonised inputs, reference frames, ephemerides, correction settings and assumptions. It would also require documented tolerances, repeated test cases and an independent assessment of the results.

The comparison is therefore presented as a preliminary numerical cross-check, not as a claim of scientific validation or certification.

6. Relevance, original contribution and potential impact

6.1 Integrated mission analysis

LUNAR CHRONOS brings together several capabilities that are available individually in existing scientific and technical environments. These include lunar mapping, SPICE-based calculations, solar geometry, Earth visibility analysis and mission-planning tools.

The project's contribution is to integrate these complementary capabilities into a single interactive environment focused on preliminary lunar mission planning.

This approach allows users to examine geographical, geometric and temporal considerations within a common application rather than treating each element as an entirely separate activity.

6.2 Original conceptual contribution

The principal original conceptual contribution is the integration of the proposed Cosmic Calendar and Universal Standard Time framework into the lunar mission-planning environment.

The 13-phase temporal framework introduces an additional way to organise mission timelines and relate activities to selected lunar environmental observations.

The project does not claim that its individual scientific calculations, mapping resources or software technologies are unprecedented. Its proposed contribution lies in the way these existing capabilities are brought together with an original temporal framework.

6.3 Potential applications

Subject to further development and validation, the approach could support the preliminary examination of lunar observation locations, comparison of solar elevation and Earth visibility conditions, exploration of time-dependent geometric visibility, organisation of mission activities and temporal references, educational demonstrations of lunar environmental and mission-planning concepts, and further research into the relationship between planetary environments and timekeeping systems.

These are potential applications and development directions, not claims of established operational performance.

7. Current limitations and scientific integrity

7.1 Scope of the current prototype

LUNAR CHRONOS is an independently developed prototype intended for preliminary exploration and mission-planning support.

It does not provide a complete landing-site certification process, an operational navigation service or a comprehensive assessment of lunar surface safety.

The selected geographical locations are reference points for analysis. They have not been certified as suitable landing sites.

7.2 Scientific and operational limitations

The current implementation has several limitations that must be taken into account.

Terrain and landing-site assessment: The application does not yet provide a complete LOLA-based terrain assessment, high-resolution hazard analysis or comprehensive three-dimensional evaluation of landing-site suitability.

Solar illumination and power: The solar elevation calculation does not constitute a complete solar power-generation model. Terrain shadows, panel orientation, irradiance, equipment efficiency, thermal effects and energy storage would require additional modelling.

Time-dependent solar analysis: A complete solar-elevation curve over the same 708-hour period used for Earth visibility analysis has not yet been implemented.

Earth visibility and communications: Geometric Earth visibility does not establish actual communications availability. Terrain obstruction, antenna orientation, spacecraft characteristics, link budgets and other communications constraints must be evaluated separately.

Terrain-aware visibility: The current Earth visibility analysis does not yet incorporate a complete terrain-aware obstruction model.

Scientific validation: The preliminary Horizons comparison is limited to selected numerical outputs and was not performed under fully harmonised computational conditions. Further independent testing is required.

7.3 Commitment to scientific integrity

The project distinguishes between implemented functionality, preliminary computational results and proposed future developments.

The use of NASA/JPL datasets and established scientific software is not presented as automatic proof of accuracy.

Further verification should identify the equations, inputs, reference frames, assumptions and correction settings used by each calculation. Results should then be compared against independent authoritative sources under documented and reproducible conditions.

Any differences should be measured against defined tolerances, with results classified as passed, requiring investigation or not yet evaluated.

This approach is intended to ensure that future development is guided by traceable evidence rather than unsupported claims.

8. Future development and progressive roadmap

The following roadmap identifies possible development directions. These activities are proposed future work and should not be interpreted as features already implemented in the current prototype.

8.1 Scientific validation and computational accuracy

The first priority is to strengthen the scientific reliability and traceability of the calculations.

Future work could include documenting equations, inputs, assumptions and computational settings; recording the exact SPICE kernels, reference frames and correction options used; comparing outputs with independent NASA/JPL reference calculations; harmonising test configurations wherever possible; establishing numerical tolerances and acceptance criteria; creating reproducible test cases for solar elevation and Earth visibility; extending independent comparisons to additional dates and lunar locations; and documenting discrepancies and their possible causes.

The objective is to establish a transparent verification process before making stronger claims about scientific accuracy.

8.2 Lunar terrain and 3D visualisation

A further development direction is to introduce more detailed lunar terrain information and three-dimensional visualisation.

Potential data sources include Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) datasets, particularly Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) topography and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) imagery.

These resources could support future terrain visualisation, elevation analysis and examination of local surface features.

A terrain-aware model could also help identify potential obstructions affecting solar illumination and geometric Earth visibility.

The integration of such data would require careful treatment of coordinate systems, spatial resolution, data quality, coverage and uncertainty.

8.3 Environmental and mission-operations analysis

Future development could extend the environmental analysis beyond the geometric parameters currently implemented.

Potential areas include surface temperature and thermal conditions, illumination duration and shadow analysis, terrain-related environmental constraints, more detailed examination of observation and operational periods, and the integration of additional environmental datasets.

NASA's Diviner Lunar Radiometer Experiment could provide a potential source of thermal information.

The Lunar Exploration Neutron Detector (LEND) and Mini-RF radar datasets could also be investigated for their relevance to future geological and resource-related analysis.

Such datasets provide scientific observations and indicators. They do not, by themselves, establish the presence of accessible or recoverable resources.

8.4 Mission planning and temporal framework

The proposed UST framework could be developed further to support more detailed mission timeline organisation.

Potential improvements include associating mission activities with UST phases while retaining UTC as the authoritative time reference, linking planned activities to selected solar elevation and Earth visibility conditions, improving the presentation of mission timelines and temporal comparisons, introducing more detailed activity scheduling and scenario management, and documenting the mathematical and temporal assumptions of the UST framework.

Any future extension would require a clearly defined temporal model and independent technical review. UST would remain a proposed framework unless formally developed and recognised through an appropriate standardisation process.

8.5 Data integration and continuous improvement

The application could progressively incorporate additional authoritative scientific datasets and services.

Potential work includes improving data provenance and source documentation, recording dataset versions and processing levels, assessing coordinate and reference-frame compatibility, managing uncertainty and data-quality information, introducing additional interfaces for scientific datasets, and improving the traceability of calculated and imported values.

Data integration should be guided by scientific relevance and technical compatibility rather than by the quantity of datasets incorporated.

8.6 Public scientific datasets and data sources

Several publicly available datasets could be considered for future development.

Lunar datasets

Potential lunar sources include LRO LOLA for topography and elevation information, LROC for surface imagery, Diviner for thermal observations, LEND for neutron measurements relevant to hydrogen distribution studies, and Mini-RF for radar observations and surface-property investigations.

Scientific and technical resources

Relevant resources could include the NASA Planetary Data System (PDS), LRO data archives, LROC data services, JPL Horizons, JPL planetary and lunar ephemerides, and NASA's Navigation and Ancillary Information Facility (NAIF) SPICE resources.

For a possible future extension beyond the Moon, Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) data could be investigated as a source of Martian topographic information.

The integration of any dataset would require assessment of its availability, resolution, calibration, coordinate system, processing level, temporal coverage and uncertainty. Public availability does not necessarily mean that datasets are directly compatible or suitable for immediate operational use.

8.7 Future planetary timekeeping and navigation

The Cosmic Calendar and proposed UST framework could provide a starting point for exploring time organisation beyond the lunar environment.

A future research direction could examine how temporal frameworks might be adapted to other planetary environments, including Mars.

Areas for investigation could include planetary rotation and local solar time, planet-specific temporal references, synchronisation between spacecraft, surface assets and mission control, integration with planetary ephemerides and SPICE-based navigation, the treatment of relativistic effects where relevant, and differences between lunar and planetary timekeeping requirements.

This is an exploratory research direction, not an implemented capability of the current LUNAR CHRONOS prototype.

8.8 Solar exposure and power-planning applications

Future development could extend the current solar elevation calculations towards a more comprehensive examination of solar exposure and potential power-planning considerations.

Potential elements include solar incidence angles on selected surfaces, duration of direct illumination, terrain-related shadow analysis, assessment of possible solar panel orientations, comparison of potential locations for energy installations, and integration of temperature and irradiance information.

A complete power model would also need to consider panel efficiency, equipment characteristics, degradation, energy storage and operational demand.

The objective would be to move progressively from geometric illumination analysis towards a more complete environmental and energy-planning assessment.

8.9 Geological analysis, resources and infrastructure

A further development direction could explore the relationship between lunar surface characteristics, geological information and potential infrastructure planning.

Possible areas of investigation include surface composition and geological context, regolith characteristics, remote-sensing indicators associated with possible water-ice deposits, terrain properties relevant to surface infrastructure, potential locations for scientific installations and other facilities, and preliminary examination of materials relevant to future construction or resource utilisation.

These applications would require appropriate scientific datasets and careful interpretation. Remote-sensing observations and indirect indicators must not be presented as proof of the existence, accessibility or economic recoverability of resources.

8.10 Planetary surface-operations dashboard

The project could eventually evolve towards a broader surface-operations dashboard.

Such an environment could bring together mission timelines, environmental conditions, location information and operational constraints.

Potential components include mission and activity timelines, surface environmental information, rover and robotic asset positions, route and location visualisation, energy status and power-planning information, communications status and constraints, and external sensor and mission-data interfaces.

This would represent a substantial future development beyond the current prototype. It would require appropriate data interfaces, reliable external inputs, validated calculations and mission-specific operational requirements.

8.11 Progressive implementation plan and development milestones

The long-term development of LUNAR CHRONOS will follow a progressive milestone-based approach. Each stage will build on the results of the previous one, with priorities determined by scientific data availability, technical feasibility and verification requirements.

Milestone 1 — Prototype consolidation and scientific verification

Priorities:

  • Stabilise the existing application and document its architecture and implemented capabilities.
  • Expand independent verification of solar and Earth geometry calculations.
  • Improve the traceability of scientific inputs, assumptions and calculation configurations.
  • Establish reproducible test cases and documented acceptance criteria.

Expected outcome: A more thoroughly documented and independently tested lunar mission-planning prototype.

Milestone 2 — Environmental and geological data integration

Priorities:

  • Evaluate and progressively integrate appropriate public LRO datasets, including LOLA topography, LROC imagery, Diviner thermal observations and relevant LEND and Mini-RF products.
  • Develop preliminary terrain, illumination, thermal-environment and geological visualisation.
  • Examine the potential relevance of surface composition, water-ice indicators and regolith characteristics.
  • Document data resolution, uncertainty, provenance and limitations.

Expected outcome: An expanded lunar environmental-analysis capability based on traceable scientific datasets, without claiming certified resource identification.

Milestone 3 — Surface suitability, energy and infrastructure planning

Priorities:

  • Develop more detailed terrain-aware illumination and shadow analysis.
  • Assess solar-panel exposure using incidence angle, illumination duration, terrain obstruction and relevant environmental conditions.
  • Progress towards preliminary comparisons of potential locations for energy systems, scientific installations, landing areas and future infrastructure.
  • Investigate the relevance of geological and surface-material information for potential construction and resource utilisation.

Expected outcome: A preliminary environment for comparing selected lunar locations in relation to terrain, illumination, energy opportunities and infrastructure considerations.

Milestone 4 — Mission and planetary surface-operations dashboard

Priorities:

  • Progressively integrate mission timelines, environmental conditions, navigation information and operational constraints.
  • Investigate suitable interfaces for future robotic vehicles, rovers and other surface systems.
  • Explore the monitoring and organisation of vehicle location, route planning, energy status, communications conditions and scheduled activities.
  • Assess the technical requirements for receiving and interpreting external vehicle and sensor data.

Expected outcome: A prototype concept for an integrated mission and surface-operations dashboard, subject to the availability of suitable interfaces and validated operational data.

Milestone 5 — Planetary adaptation and extended timekeeping research

Priorities:

  • Investigate the adaptation of the proposed UST temporal concept to Mars and other planetary environments.
  • Examine planetary rotation, local solar time, precise clock synchronisation, navigation requirements and relativistic effects.
  • Explore relevant public planetary datasets, ephemerides and SPICE resources.
  • Assess which elements of the lunar mission-planning architecture could be reused and which would require planet-specific development.

Expected outcome: A documented feasibility framework for potential planetary extensions, rather than a claim of an operational multi-planetary system.

Milestone verification and implementation principles

Each milestone will be subject to a review of scientific data quality, technical feasibility, computational accuracy and remaining uncertainties. Progression to the next stage will depend on documented results rather than assumptions of completion.

The proposed milestones are development objectives. Their timing and scope will depend on available resources, data compatibility, independent verification and the technical requirements identified during implementation.

9. Use of super-intelligence tools and AI-assisted development

9.1 Original concept and project direction

The original concept, project direction and principal design decisions behind LUNAR CHRONOS were developed by N. Sahra.

The Cosmic Calendar and proposed Universal Standard Time framework originated from the project's own conceptual foundation.

The use of artificial intelligence tools did not replace the original project concept or the responsibility for its development.

9.2 AI-assisted technical development

Artificial intelligence tools, including ChatGPT and other software-assisted resources, were used during parts of the development process.

Their assistance included research and information gathering, technical explanations and exploration of implementation approaches, coding assistance, debugging and troubleshooting, data analysis and interpretation, and documentation drafting, editing and refinement.

These tools supported the development process but did not independently establish the scientific validity of the application's calculations.

9.3 Human responsibility and scientific verification

Responsibility for the project concept, development choices, implementation decisions, review and final project content remains with the project developer.

AI-generated suggestions and technical outputs require human assessment, particularly when they relate to scientific calculations, data interpretation and mission-planning claims.

The use of AI assistance is therefore disclosed as part of the development process, without presenting it as a substitute for independent scientific verification.

10. Conclusion — from a lunar prototype to a broader planetary vision

LUNAR CHRONOS represents the first practical implementation of an original concept developed to bring lunar mission planning, environmental observation and time organisation together within a single framework.

The current prototype combines interactive lunar mapping, SPICE-based calculations, solar elevation analysis, Earth visibility geometry, time-dependent visibility analysis, selected mission references and a proposed 13-phase temporal framework.

Its principal conceptual contribution is the integration of these complementary capabilities with the proposed Cosmic Calendar and Universal Standard Time framework.

The project is deliberately presented as a prototype rather than a completed operational system. Its scientific outputs require further independent verification, and its current capabilities do not constitute certified landing-site safety assessments or complete operational communications and power-planning models.

The next stages of development will focus on scientific validation, improved terrain and environmental analysis, additional scientific data integration and more detailed mission-planning capabilities.

Beyond its immediate lunar focus, the project also opens a broader research direction: exploring how environmental observation, mission planning and proposed temporal frameworks could be considered together in future planetary exploration.

11. Looking ahead

LUNAR CHRONOS began with a specific objective: to explore how lunar location, environmental conditions and mission timelines could be considered together within a single planning environment.

The project also raises a broader question about how time should be organised and interpreted when human and robotic activities extend beyond Earth. The proposed Cosmic Calendar and UST framework offer an original starting point for exploring this question, while retaining UTC as the authoritative reference in the current application.

The immediate priority is to strengthen the lunar prototype through independent verification, improved scientific data integration and more detailed environmental analysis. Further development could then explore additional applications in surface operations, energy planning, infrastructure assessment and planetary navigation.

The longer-term ambition is to investigate whether the underlying approach could be adapted to other planetary environments, while recognising that each body requires its own scientific, temporal and operational models.

These possibilities remain research and development objectives. Their implementation will depend on technical feasibility, authoritative data, independent validation and the resources available.

LUNAR CHRONOS is therefore both a practical first implementation and the beginning of a wider research direction: bringing scientific observation, mission planning and an original temporal concept into a coherent framework for planetary exploration.

LUNAR CHRONOS

Explore the Moon. Plan with precision.
